activity_script_v1_1: Campus police operated Driving Under the Influence checkpoints, with backing from the local city police and the highway patrol. Checkpoints were conducted on three main streets surrounding the campus. These streets were selected because they had a significant amount of student foot traffic and motor vehicle traffic. On average, 730 cars were stopped at each checkpoint. The primary goal of the checkpoints was to increase the perception of risk of arrest for Driving Under the Influence. Arrests were a secondary goal. As such, the checkpoints covered 10-15 officers, several police cars with their lights turned on, cones, flares and large spotlights. On average, each Driving Under the Influence checkpoint cost $3000 (US) to operate.
barriers_v1_1_v2: Implementing driving under the influence (DUI) checkpoints is labour- and resource-intensive. A typical operation would require up to ten police officers and substantial overtime pay. In addition, although the project staff had a longstanding professional relationship with law enforcement, the activity still required considerable coordination.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: Implementing a roadside checkpoint campaign may be particularly difficult in a context where the community does not already have a public safety department responsible for conducting this activity. In addition, it was crucial for the project staff to have a good working relationship with law enforcement.

activity_delivery_details: Almost all of the students (97%) completed at least one Slick Tracy booklet, with 85% completing most of the booklets (three to four).

facilitators_v1_1_v2: Incentives were found to be helpful to encourage engagement with the teacher training. Students received pens after completion of the first 2 weeks of activities.
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: The authors considered that, as the school staff were willing to participate during a "time of social and economic hardship", this demonstrated that the school staff supported the activity.

reference: Werch, C. E., et al. (2003). "One-year follow-up results of the STARS for Families alcohol prevention program." Health education research Vol.18(1): 74-87p.
activity_script_v1_1: Trained nurses provided health consultations using standardised protocols. The registered nurse consultations offered stage-matched prevention messages, identifying risk/protective factors, the purpose of the risk communication, prevention messages addressing the identified risk/protective factors and a nurse recommendation contract asking the child to avoid future alcohol use. A protocol covered directions for implementing the consultation including perceived susceptibility and severity; perceived benefits; cues to avoid alcohol; motivation and intentions; the environment and influenceability; self-efficacy and behavioural capability; situation (perceived prevalence); expectations; expectancies; emotional coping responses; observational learning; and self evaluation, self-monitoring and self-reinforcement.
barriers_v1_1_v2: The authors suggested that the activity may have been 'less effective due to tailoring the content to too many risk and protective factors'.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: The authors cite a study that found "good fitting nontailored materials" to have a comparable, and even greater, impact than tailored materials. For example, the authors went on to describe that "earlier studies that were tailored to stage of initiation, and not to risk and protective factors, had greater impact".
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: Student feedback showed high satisfaction with the nurse consultations, with 93–98% of intervention students rating them favourably across seven process measures, compared to 83–98% of control group students regarding their materials. Nurse feedback was similarly positive, with 87–97% evaluating their consultations favourably across three measures. Additionally, independent research staff and school nurse staff both rated taped consultations consistently high (80–100% in favor) for accuracy, effectiveness, enthusiasm, responsiveness, and smoothness.

activity_script_v1_1: Physician-endorsed mailed prevention postcards were addressed to the parent or guardian of participating youth that provided a set of brief activities for parents/guardians and children to complete together. Postcards were based on youth stage status and the number of risk/protective factors pinpointed during annual preintervention data collections. The risk/protective factors addressed were the same as in the health consultations, and covered perceived benefits, cues to avoid alcohol, and motivation and intentions; perceived susceptibility and severity; environment and influenceability; situation (perceived prevalence); expectations; expectancies; self-efficacy and behavioural capability; self evaluation, self-monitoring and self-reinforcement; observational learning; and emotional coping responses.
activity_delivery_details: Almost all parents talked with their child about individual take-home lessons (94 - 98%). In addition, almost all parents signed contracts attached to individual take-home lessons that students returned to school (92 - 97%).
barriers_v1_1_v2: The activity may have been less effective due to tailoring the content to too many risk and protective factors. Earlier studies that were tailored to stage of initiation, and not to risk and protective factors, had greater impact.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: Print materials were chosen to reduce the need for expensive resources and to reduce demand on teachers.
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: Almost all parents reported that they would recommend the take-home lessons.

activity_script_v1_1: The Responsible Beverage Service component was designed to increase compliance with existing alcohol policies through a combination of measures: obtaining sponsorship and backing from local and state hospitality organisations, offering manager and server training for all on- and off premise licensed alcohol outlets in the selected neighbourhoods using a standard curriculum, developing a process to increase enforcement of existing laws regarding service to intoxicated customers, and obtaining endorsement of Responsible Beverage Service from neighbourhood bodies and organisations. Which focused on (1) raising awareness of the problems of youthful drinking and the sale of alcohol to minors and intoxicated persons; (2) raising awareness of community norms against the sale of alcohol to minors and intoxicated persons; (3) training in methods of age identification, estimating intoxication levels, and techniques for interacting with customers; (4) offering information about laws and associated penalties for sales to minors and intoxicated persons; and (5) reviewing with owners and managers existing policies and offering new policy options to reduce sales to minors and intoxicated persons.
activity_delivery_details: Participation in responsible beverage service (RBS) training varied across sites. In the South site, staff from 40% of on-premise outlets (n = 52) and 69% of off-premise outlets (n = 54) attended training, while in the North site participation was slightly higher, with staff from 56% of on-premise outlets (n = 45) and 70% of off-premise outlets (n = 37) taking part.

activity_script_v1_1: Parenting Adolescents: a Creative Experience' involved eight 2-hour group sessions for parents and caregivers. The program was facilitated by a trained parent educator and covered topics on listening, assertion, adolescent development, conflict resolution, resilience, drugs and alcohol, and family. Existing policies and practices for parent engagement at the school were reviewed and this created opportunities for parents and caregivers to build backing networks in the early years of secondary school. In addition, there was schoolwide distribution of a handbook for parents and caregivers, combining evidence-based information and practical parenting strategies. A brief parent information and learning evening facilitated by an adolescent-health expert was also implemented. This involved a 2-hour Parenting Adolescents Quiz offering a fun social evening for parents and caregivers to work together and learn ways to prompt healthy adolescent development by addressing topics such as youth culture, communication, depression, sibling rivalry, alcohol and drugs, and conflict resolution.
activity_delivery_details: A minority of parents participated in the brief parent education evening (12%) or the extended parent education sessions (6%). Because of low response from parents, the program failed to implement an initiative for parents to exchange contact information.

activity_script_v1_1: Information was provided at parents' sessions once per year, directly subsequent to the completion of a self-report survey. The information provided at these parents' sessions covered: 1) up to date information on alcohol, tobacco and drug use among students in the municipality (e.g., the prevalence of alcohol consumption and drunkenness, what types of beverages the adolescents usually drink and how they get hold of the alcohol); 2) information on risks associated with youth drinking in the form of risks for immediate (acute) harms, risks for long-term harms (e.g., that an early alcohol debut was associated with an increased risk of developing alcohol problems), and the linked between alcohol and other drugs; and 3) advice to parents on what they could do to prevent and discourage their children from drinking alcohol. In addition, newsletters were sent via e-mail 3-6 times per year to parents and to other adults who registered to receive them. The emails provided up to date information on the alcohol and drug situation among youths in the municipality, for example information in connection with public holidays and similar occasions that may be associated with partying among young people. These newsletters presented results and more in-depth analyses from the self-report surveys.

activity_script_v1_1: students were trained in the various Life Skills Training through the use of interactive teaching techniques, covering coaching, facilitating, role modelling, results feedback, and reinforcement, plus homework exercises and out-of-class behavioural rehearsal. The cognitive component was designed to present information concerning the immediate and longer term consequences of substance use, current adolescent and adult prevalence rates of substance use, social acceptability of substance use, the process of becoming a user, development of substance use addiction, and media influences on behaviour. Specific content was contained in four sessions on substance use information and one session on media influences.
activity_delivery_details: Independent observations of classroom delivery indicated that teachers implemented the Life Skills Training (LST) program with high fidelity. Observers reported an average adherence of 85% to the curriculum during the initial program and 82% during the booster sessions approximately one year later, with acceptable agreement between observers (78% and 71%, respectively).

activity_script_v1_1: The seven Strengthening Family Partnerships program sessions were conducted weekly when the youth were in the second semester of seventh grade. In addition, a concurrent one-hour parent and youth skills-building curriculum, followed by a one-hour conjoint family curriculum was developed during which parents and youth practiced skills learned in their separate sessions. Each session was offered in the participating schools during the evening. Parent and family sessions used discussions, skill-building activities, videotapes that modelled positive behaviour, and games designed to build skills and strengthen positive interactions among family members. The program was based on the biopsychosocial model and other empirically based family risk and protective factor models.
activity_delivery_details: Attendance at the Strengthening Families Program 10–14 (SFP 10–14) was high, with 88% of families attending at least four of the seven sessions and 63% attending at least six. Independent observations indicated excellent implementation fidelity, with facilitators delivering 92–98% of the planned content across family, parent, and youth sessions. Similar levels of fidelity were maintained during the booster sessions conducted one year later, with high agreement between observers.

activity_script_v1_1: To maximise the likelihood of high community attendance, four street dramas were performed on government holidays and in the evening when most of the village could be in attendance. Each performance presented information on the negative consequences of alcohol use and were preceded by the actors moving through the village dancing, singing and leading the community to the village communal area. Preparation and a performance for the street drama were by the Department of Fine Arts under the supervision of the Department of Psychiatry, University of Peradeniya.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: Organising dry events on government holidays and in the evening was thought to increase community participation as "most of the village" was thought to be at home. The use of locally produced drama increased the support and cultural acceptance of the activity. The community events were reported to be the primary motivation for the formation of a community group which encouraged females to take significant roles.
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: Most of the community members approved of the street dramas (75%). In fact, the community was motivated to hold an additional two street dramas.

activity_script_v1_1: Posters were designed in a locally familiar style that was used for important community events such as festivals. They highlighted how negative consequences to the human body, economy and society could be overcome by moderating one's drinking. These posters were placed in commonly frequented areas of the villages. Additional leaflets focused upon alcohol-drinking patterns, its consequences and when people should seek medical advice. Alcohol dependence was defined as a disease and emphasised safe levels of alcohol consumption and avoidance of high concentration alcoholic beverages such as kasippu. These were hand-delivered to each household.

activity_script_v1_1: A free medical clinic was held in each village on a public holiday to increase access. Blood tests were taken for liver functioning, creatinine and blood sugar and the results were supplied to the individuals' normal health care provider. Individuals who were pinpointed as high-risk drinkers received a brief prevention activity given by the attending doctor. In addition, village drinkers whose Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test (AUDIT) score placed them in either the harmful or dependent category were offered a the brief prevention activity. This activity focussed on harm minimization and safer drinking patterns.

activity_script_v1_1: The youth prevention activity consisted of 32 television messages and 23 radio messages produced to appeal to the interests and needs of youth in the targeted age group. Concepts were rated for coverage of objectives and potential appeal to youth by an expert panel consisting of eight alcohol prevention specialists, psychologists, health educators, and communication/media consultants. Educational objectives for young people were: 1) increased positive expectations for nondrinking and increased negative expectations for drinking; 2) more realistic perceptions of drinking prevalence among peer groups; 3) perceiving increased backing for nondrinking from peers and parents; 4) increased confidence in ability to avoid alcohol use; and 5) perceiving reduced access to alcohol.
activity_delivery_details: The media campaign delivered approximately 10 television and five radio advertisements each year, with an average of 260 broadcast television, 1,040 cable television, and 950 radio placements annually. Media outlets also contributed an additional 50% in public service airtime, resulting in an estimated 300 gross rating points (GRPs), equivalent to an average of three exposures per week for the target audience over nine months each year for three years, and six months in the fourth year. In total, less than half of the youth (43%) reported seeing the television messages, or heard the radio messages (37%).
barriers_v1_1_v2: Media campaigns may suffer from insufficient dedicated resources to ensure the design and development of effective messaging and the required threshold intensity of media placements. In addition, media campaigns often lack sufficient engagement with the community, particularly youth, due to the use of multiple media channels and the ability to bypass advertisements with paid services. Finally, any messaging against the drinking culture may be easily overcome by the substantial resourcing of significant and appealing advertisements from the alcohol industry, which reinforces positive expectations.
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: Of those who saw the media campaign, most reported liking the messaging (75%).

activity_script_v1_1: This component was designed to increase adolescents' coping, self-regulation and school engagement. Active learning strategies were designed to teach a range of social-cognitive coping skills to manage family, school, peer, and culturally-linked stressors, covering situations involving risk-taking and pressures to drink. The skills were taught using methods to increase efficacy from previous studies in mental health and focussed on social competence and cognitive problem-solving as well as emotion awareness, emotion focused coping, and cognitive reframing techniques shown to be effective in reducing depressive symptoms.

activity_script_v1_1: The prevention activity employed active listening and a four-stage skills training strategy (skill description, modelling, in-session and home Practice, and results feedback). This activity was designed to increase: 1) parents' use of effective parenting practices; 2) positive family bonds and relationships; and 3) parents' promotion of school engagement. Special focus was afforded on listening skills to strengthen parental responsiveness and backing, and positive reinforcement to prompt youth effort and positive development, appropriate discipline (clear rules and consistent consequences to offer structure and to minimise harsh parenting), and adequate monitoring to offer ongoing supervision of academic progress and to limit adolescents' unsupervised interactions with deviant peers). The activity comprised nine weekly group sessions on school grounds and two home visits. The sessions were delivered separately to the adolescents and parents (1.25 hours) and together (0.75 hours).
activity_delivery_details: The project staff reported that 88% of the activity was implemented.

barriers_v1_1_v2: The cultivation of partnerships was hampered by a historical lack of collaboration between the partners (neighbourhood associations and the university). This meant that sustaining the partnerships required significant resourcing to maintain the network. In addition, the membership was in a state of continual flux as much of the membership was based on a student population that was likely to change priorities and was in need of training in conflict management and mediation. Despite offering this training, it was ultimately not possible to maintain the partnerships.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: The project staff identified four elements that were found to support the formation of partnerships. First, having existing organisations with established communication channels. Second, having the ability to 'map' the geographic distribution of youth to aid with focussing efforts. Third, having the means to engage with young people in the locations they frequent. Finally, placing an emphasis on sustainable action.

activity_script_v1_1: The School Health and Alcohol Harm Reduction Project (SHAHRP) curriculum. SHAHRP is a resistance skills training program and covered elements of alcohol-specific personal and social skills training. It covered three main strategies: 1) teaching students to recognise high-risk situations; 2) increasing the awareness of external influences on behaviour; and 3) combining self-control (ie, the ability to control responses, to interrupt undesired behavioural tendencies and refrain from acting on them) with refusal skills training (ie, to improve self-efficacy in avoiding unhealthy behaviours).

activity_script_v1_1: Smoking prevention curriculum involved ten sessions delivered across two weeks. Major elements addressed in the first week sessions were: (a) correction of norms (particularly misperceptions of the prevalence of tobacco use among adolescents and in the general population); (b) awareness of peer influences to smoke; (c) development of peer resistance skills; (f) instruction on the social and physiological consequences of smoking; and (g) development of decision-making skills. Elements addressed in the second week of sessions were: (a) motivations for smoking; (b) adult, advertising and media influences; and (c) assertiveness and nonsmoker's rights.
activity_delivery_details: There was substantial variability in the fidelity of classroom program delivery. Fidelity was assessed through instructors' adherence to the curriculum during role plays and the quality of delivery. An Integrity Index (range: 1.4–15.3) combined adherence, use of the Socratic method, and role-play leadership skills. Instructor scores ranged from 4.04 to 12.65 (mean = 9.27), indicating considerable variation in implementation quality. Higher integrity scores were associated with more animated, articulate, and confident delivery, as well as a less authoritarian teaching style.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: The project staff piloted the school activities and following initial feedback they decided to decrease emphasis on exercise, diet, and relaxation tips, and place more emphasis on self-talk, recycling, social support processes, and trigger situations. In addition, the school staff were encouraged to reciprocate by modelling smoke-free behaviours.
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: Teachers shared a preference for social resistance curriculum that included classroom skills demonstration. Health instructors and students reported high acceptance overall.

reference: Flay BR, Miller TQ, Hedeker D, Siddiqui O, Britton CF, Brannon BR, et al. The television, school, and family smoking prevention and cessation project. VIII. Student outcomes and mediating variables. Prev Med. 1995;24(1):29-40.
activity_script_v1_1: The media campaign included three week television programming (a KABC-TV "Feeling Fine" program) for social resistance skills and applying assertive pressure to quit smoking and social support to do so (week one), resistance to social influences, tobacco advertising and Industry tactics as well as self efficacy (week two), and thoughtful decision making and the promotion of social activism (week three). The program was developed by project staff and staff from the KABC-TV affiliate to align with a school curriculum and encouraged discussion of health issues and was aired in the local evening news, Monday through Friday.
activity_delivery_details: The television segments did not meet the research objectives, particularly because they lacked a progressive and detailed demonstration of social resistance skills.
barriers_v1_1_v2: The media campaign was developed in collaboration between research staff and a commercial news organisation. As the news organisation had certain contract restraints, programming that had been demonstrated to be effective, such as showing substance-use resistance techniques, could not be shown. The media staff and project staff each had different expectations. The media staff, due to trade union restrictions, could not allow project staff to participate during shooting or editing and generally would not allow coaching of participants instead of filming in natural settings (which itself became an issue when there was inclement weather). In addition, the media staff were assigned to the project "randomly", so it was difficult to establish a working relationship.
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: The evaluation indicated that an average of half a million households, or about 650,000 people, would have seen the project media campaign.

activity_script_v1_1: Tobacco retailers in close proximity to schools or major thoroughfares to schools were targeted to receive two monthly controlled purchase operations (CPOs) (initially this was once or twice a year but this was found to be less effective) delivered by the Auckland Regional Public Health Service.
activity_delivery_details: The proportion of retailers who were visited by law enforcement was lower than was planned. Across the communities, less than half to two-thirds of the retailers were visited.
barriers_v1_1_v2: Tobacco vendors were warned of the compliance checking and this may have reduced the effectiveness of the activity.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: To better reflect practice, the project staff used both supervised and unsupervised minors when conducting the enforcement checks. Unsupervised minors were instructed to lie about their age, use false ID, dress to appear older and act to cajole a clerk into making a sale. In contrast, the supervised minors were instructed to dress in age-appropriate clothes, tell the truth about their age and say that the cigarettes were for their personal use.
participation_v1_1_v2: When warned of possible compliance checking, vendors were more likely to sell to familiar minors. As the supervised minors who conducted the checks were strangers to the vendors, the vendors may have been hesitant to sell to them.

activity_script_v1_1: Interactive classroom program for grades seven to nine that were delivered across five to eight one hour sessions. The program addressed decision making, resistance skills, and health consequences of smoking. All activities were delivered by teachers in the normal classroom context but involved the use of video, games, and group work.
barriers_v1_1_v2: Student feedback identified that the main messaging of the curriculum had become repetitive and "sufficiently emphasised". In addition, students with poor academic performance may have found the curriculum insufficiently structured and perhaps also too difficult and demanding.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: The activity was designed following extensive engagement with selected experts, teachers, parents and students, and was piloted before community-wide implementation. Following this engagement, the most important considerations were that the activity be adjusted to fit in the existing classroom programs by emphasising simplicity, well-known pedagogical methods, and demands for low-cost audio-visual equipment only. In addition, the activity had high levels of student involvement and focussed on non-smoking as a kind of freedom.
participation_v1_1_v2: The authors hypothesised that school prevention activities would have a greater impact when delivered to all grades rather than to a single grade cohort.

facilitators_v1_1_v2: Tobacco Free Duo was designed as a long-term, systems-based intervention that sought to prevent smoking by addressing both individual and social influences. The program combined school, peer, family, and broader community involvement to create a supportive environment in which remaining tobacco-free became the expected social norm. Central to the approach was empowering young people to make their own commitment to remain tobacco-free while actively involving them in the intervention's design and delivery to ensure it reflected their experiences. Peer support was strengthened through tobacco-free partnerships, reinforcing healthy social identities and positive norms. The program emphasised sustained implementation, integration into everyday school and community life, and strong local ownership, while allowing adaptation to local contexts provided the core components of the intervention were maintained.

barriers_v1_1_v2: The tobacco industry substantially increased its expenditure to directly oppose the prevention activities, encourage and support minority organisations to oppose the programme, and make campaign contributions to legislators. facilitators_v1_1_v2: Successful policy-based tobacco prevention requires coordinated advocacy that combines political influence, strategic planning, and effective leadership. The initiative relied on mobilising strong public support to influence political decision-making, while ensuring advocates had a clear, evidence-informed vision for how funding should be allocated to address tobacco-related harms. Success also depended on communicating a simple, compelling message that resonated with decision-makers and the public—in this case, emphasising that implementation should reflect the will of voters. Recognising and managing competing interests from organisations seeking the same funding was also important, requiring advocates to maintain a consistent policy narrative. Overall, the policy activities highlighted the importance of strategic leadership, clear policy goals, effective message framing, and the ability to capitalise on political opportunities to achieve and sustain policy change.

activity_delivery_details: Parent participation was generally low. Although 6,500 questionnaires were distributed, only 1,738 were returned at baseline and 329 at follow-up. Few parents engaged with the broader activities: five registered for the information evening and nine contacted the Quit telephone service. However, 73 parents expressed interest in reducing cigarette sales to minors, and 24 of the 30 active participants interviewed reported taking part in at least one related activity. activity_script_v1_1: An in-school media campaign, "Be Under Your Own Influence". This campaign was designed through social marketing principles that encouraged local development and a focus on influencing behaviour change by addressing smoking attitudes and values (feelings of rebellious noncompliance and independence). Thus substance use, primarily cannabis but also tobacco and alcohol, was framed as being inconsistent with achieving independence. The campaign included print materials such as a series of posters as well as promotional items such as book covers, tray liners, T-shirts, water bottles, rulers and lanyards. Images of healthy but risky activities such as rock-climbing and four-wheeling were used to target risk-oriented, sensation-seeking youth. The campaign was monitored via qualitative and quantitative process evaluations several times throughout campaign implementation and adaptations were made as needed.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: Nursing home visits provided an important foundation for successful mentoring. By developing students' interpersonal skills and fostering understanding of older adults through both classroom learning and nursing home experiences, the program created the conditions needed for positive and meaningful interactions between students and their older mentors.
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: Although many students were anxious prior to meeting with their mentor or visiting nursing homes, this feeling tended to subside once the students took part.

activity_script_v1_1: Middle school students in sixth grade were paired with a mentor (an older adult aged 55 and over) and the duo was encouraged to meet for at least four hours per week to support school work and engage in activities such as eating meals, visiting shopping centres, visiting nursing homes and going to the movies. Some of these activities were incentivised through the provision of free transport or grocery vouchers to encourage participation. In addition, group events were arranged by program staff.
activity_delivery_details: The students visited a chosen nursing home approximately ten to twelve times during the school year (visiting approximately every two to three weeks).
barriers_v1_1_v2: Different students have different learning styles and needs. As a result, the school activities, which were limited to a single school year, may not have been effective for high-risk students who may be more likely to respond and engage with activities over time or at multiple points in time.
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: Students, teachers, and parents reported "liking" the activities. The authors stated that the activities "changed the dynamics of the school environment for many students".

activity_delivery_details: A total of 115 families (23% of all eligible families) participated, and of these families, 88 were referred on to receive additional support. On average, the families participated in 8.9 hours of contact with activity staff.

In addition, during summer holidays, youths were offered eight weekly sessions of structured programming and ongoing interaction with their coaches who acted to support the students during the holiday period. In addition, the coaches hosted a two-day overnight visit to local university campus including access to tailored classes and workshops.

activity_script_v1_1: Parents were offered six weekly interactive sessions, delivered in collaboration with school staff; the Unidos Family Workshop Series. The sessions were designed to help parents better understand the education system and foster their child's academic success.

satistfaction_v1_1_v2: Almost all of the participants (95%) reported satisfaction with both the activity content and delivery following each session. At the end of the sessions, the parents and youth "revealed strong enthusiasm for the Unidos program".

activity_script_v1_1: Project staff (assisted by school teachers) led 20, one hour, twice weekly, classroom sessions. The sessions included role-play, social and problem solving skills, group work, free play to promote positive peer interactions, and daily rewards for prosocial behaviour or avoiding negative behaviour during the free play. The second session each week also included a formal class problem solving activity. Content was tailored for first- and fifth-grade students. Toward the end of sessions for fifth grade students there was an additional focus of preparing for middle school. The sessions are designed so that they can be delivered by classroom teachers, school counsellors, psychologists, or trained paraprofessionals.
activity_delivery_details: Almost all students (90% on average) participated in the social and problem-solving skills sessions and associated recesses.

activity_script_v1_1: Parents received weekly newsletters, teacher-parent sessions, and a dedicated phone line staffed by project staff within the student's classroom.
activity_delivery_details: Almost all families (93%) participated in at least one parenting activity, although less than one third (28%) attended all six group sessions.
participation_v1_1_v2: The primary source of parenting information (i.e., four or more sessions via the same source) was 58% group, 15% mail, 9% none, and 6% individual.

activity_script_v1_1: All grades one through ten received a teacher-led curriculum which focussed on developing social-cognitive skills to improve social and emotional competence (the "Fast Track PATHS" (Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies)). The sessions reduced in frequency over the school years, with weekly sessions in grade one, every two weeks in grade two, and then once a month. In grade five and six, the sessions focussed on drug and alcohol use, decision making, and transitioning into middle school. Parents were invited to attend these sessions. In grades seven and eight the curriculum included forums on career pathways, essential life skills, and employment opportunities. In grades seven through ten the curriculum was more individualised and focussed on parental supervision, peer relationships, academic performance, and social-cognitive development. In addition, in grades six through ten the students also participated in the "Oyserman's School-to-Jobs possible-selves intervention" which focussed on exploring their emerging identities.
activity_delivery_details: Almost all students participated in the activities throughout grades seven through ten (a minimum attendance rate of 80% of students).
facilitators_v1_1_v2: Consistency in implementation was supported through the use of standardised manuals, ongoing cross-site training sessions, and weekly clinical supervision.

reference: Dodge KA, Bierman KL, Coie JD, Greenberg MT, Lochman JE, McMahon RJ, Pinderhughes EE. Impact of early intervention on psychopathology, crime, and well-being at age 25. Am J Psychiatry. 2015;172(1):59-70.
activity_script_v1_1: Parents were able to attend specific sessions of the school program (Fast Track PATHS (Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies) and participate in groups with their children in the school. These sessions focussed on adolescent development, substance use (including alcohol, tobacco, and drugs), and decision-making skills. Parents were also offered home visits to address individual needs.
activity_delivery_details: Almost all families (96%) attended at least one group session, and most (79%) attended half of the sessions. Some families were reported to relocate, causing a drop in participation over time.
participation_v1_1_v2: High intervention fidelity was ensured by manualisation, regular cross-site training, and weekly clinical supervision. Outside interventions were neither encouraged nor discouraged.

activity_script_v1_1: The curriculum (Project ALERT) was designed for students in sixth and seventh grade, based on social influence approaches and focusses on how beliefs and attitudes influence healthy choices (health belief model), social influences (social learning theory), and resistance skills (self-efficacy theory). The curriculum emphasises student interaction through discussions and group activities. In seventh grade there is a focus on alcohol (including games and facts relating to alcohol-related harms) and tobacco cessation(individual and group activities to build motivation and skills to quit smoking).
activity_delivery_details: The participating teachers reported delivering 1,446 lessons, covering more than 88% of the intended content in grades seven and eight.
barriers_v1_1_v2: A small proportion of the lessons (9%) were interrupted by external events such as fire drills, school announcements, or shortened class periods.
participation_v1_1_v2: The authors noted that the teachers "rushed the delivery" in 40% of the 7th-grade lessons and 31% of the 8th-grade lessons. There was a trend for the lessons to be more likely to be delivered as intended as the teachers became more experienced with the activities.

activity_script_v1_1: A series of 12 one-hour teacher-led classroom lessons. The first four lessons focussed on student knowledge and attitudes of legal and illegal substances. Students were quizzed on the composition and health effects of substances, as well as motivations to use drugs and personal, physical, and social risk and protective factors. The fifth to eighth lessons focussed on student interpersonal skills and normative beliefs. Small group collaborative role-play exercises were utilised to build resistance skills and problem solving techniques. The last four sessions focussed on intrapersonal skill development, refusal skills, assertiveness techniques and coping strategies. The students were introduced to a five-step decision-making process and encouraged to consider different short-term and long-term personal objectives.

The selected peer pairs also were provided with a guidebook containing practical advice on managing group discussions which could be used if the peers had trouble creating a relaxed and informal environment.
barriers_v1_1_v2: The students invited to participate as peer leaders (aged 12-14 years) may not have had the required level of development and maturity that was demanded by the peer-led activities.

activity_script_v1_1: Students were organised into groups based on having a mix of different listening and comprehension abilities. The curriculum focussed on behaviour management strategies, reading and writing, critical thinking and mathematics. A series of weekly classroom meetings encouraged collaborative problem-solving by incorporating the "Good Behaviour Game" (GBG). The GBG aims to increase positive behaviours and engagement and reduce disruptive behaviours by introducing an accumulative reward system. Rewards can be exchanged for classroom privileges, stickers, or small items. In addition, disengaged students were offered small-group exercises and tutoring to suit their different learning styles and promote opportunities for positive interactions.

reference: Furr-Holden CD, Ialongo NS, Anthony JC, Petras H, Kellam SG. Developmentally inspired drug prevention: middle school outcomes in a school-based randomized prevention trial. Drug Alcohol Depend. 2004;73(2):149-58.
activity_script_v1_1: Teachers and school-based mental health staff were offered a 60 hour training to support effective curriculum implementation. In addition, the teachers could attend monthly meetings to debrief on sessions but were also monitored and provided feedback. Finally, the teachers were offered manuals, and a range of practical tools, including step-by-step guides and checklists outlining required materials, key topics, and specific tasks for each session.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: Using existing school personnel as the primary implementers helped ensure sustainability, as trained staff remained within the school system after the research period ended, increasing the likelihood that the program would continue.

activity_delivery_details: Participation in the Bridges/Puentes program was moderate, with 64% of families attending at least five of the nine sessions and 33% attending all nine sessions. Non-attendance was also lower among Spanish-speaking families (11.3%) than English-speaking families (22.8%). activity_script_v1_1: The "Keeping it R.E.A.L." ("Refuse, Explain, Avoid, and Leave") curriculum was a teacher-led ten-week program designed to strengthen drug resistance and refusal skills, foster negative attitudes toward substance use, and build life competencies such as decision-making and communication skills, personal strengths and cultural identity. The curriculum incorporates storytelling, narratives, and live and recorded performance-based approaches grounded in culture (Mexican American youth, African American and European American cultural contexts or a multicultural version combining both these cultures) to increase engagement and understanding of different social norms.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: Early research identified four approaches commonly used by adolescents to refuse substances: saying no directly, providing an explanation, avoiding risky situations, and leaving environments where substances are present. These strategies formed the REAL acronym, later expressed by students as "Keeping it R.E.A.L." Although all versions of the curriculum included these strategies, different strategies were emphasised depending on cultural relevance and research findings. The curriculum content was shaped using real-life resistance stories and communication styles from participating adolescents, along with relevant cultural values. These stories also informed the creation of video materials used in several lessons, featuring performances by local high school students. The videos demonstrated effective resistance behaviours in realistic settings, using relatable characters. Classroom activities then reinforced these lessons through culturally relevant scenarios and practice exercises. In this way, narrative theory influenced both the structure and content of the program, contributing to its effectiveness in initial testing.

activity_script_v1_1: The participating schools introduced a new teacher-led curriculum comprising 20 to 30 lessons, designed to be delivered to each year level from Kindergarten to Year 12. The lessons focused on substance use resilience, peer norms, expectations, perceptions of risk, and cultural identity and values. By delivering the curriculum across all school years, it was hoped that it would encourage school bonding by fostering a classroom environment that nurtured students and their culture.
activity_delivery_details: Project staff noted discrepancies in the extent to which teachers delivered the curriculum. Some followed the protocol, while others required additional training to maintain fidelity to the program.
barriers_v1_1_v2: During the course of the activity, staff turnover was an issue. This concern reflects broader issues affecting teachers of Native American youth.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: The project staff provided the curriculum and training to the schools for free (the broader prevention program was grant funded).

reference: Petoskey, E. L., Van Stelle, K. R., & De Jong, J. A. (1998). Prevention Through Empowerment in a Native American Community. Drugs & Society, 12(1–2), 147–162.
activity_script_v1_1: Teachers received a 24-hour training course on the new curriculum. The training directly involved teachers and assisted them in developing individual lesson plans adapted to their own classes. In addition, Elders organised an 'inservice training' with teachers and spoke about their grandchildren, shared stories, explained their concerns, discussed their views on appropriate discipline, and participated in a question-and-answer session. Finally, the teachers were invited to dinners held in their honour where Elders formally entrusted them with the care of their  grandchildren.
activity_delivery_details: Teacher turnover was a noted issue and required numerous additional training sessions throughout the implementation period.

activity_script_v1_1: The 54-lesson curriculum was designed to be delivered sequentially over 12 weeks. The curriculum was based on eight teaching strategies: 1) refusal skill training; 2) peer leader-delivered messages; 3) involvement of a parent or adult in homework to encourage family discussions; 4) health advocacy; 5) short-term risks of substance use; 6) media influence training; 7) making public commitments to healthy behaviours; and 8) emphasising peer norms by providing factual formation about health behaviours within each school. The curriculum was designed to be enjoyable, practical and hands-on, using a variety of activities and a balance of large-group, small-group, individual and cooperative learning. Teachers were asked not to talk at students for more than 7–8 minutes at a time, while an incentive system encouraged very high levels of student participation and the development of a positive peer culture. Approximately one third of the curriculum relied heavily on the use of peer leaders. Each class elected three peer leaders who were chosen due to their social influence rather than academic skills.
activity_delivery_details: Fidelity testing found that the activity was implemented as intended.
barriers_v1_1_v2: The curriculum was provided to a single grade in the whole school which may have limited any effect on normative social perceptions. In addition, there was some resistance from parent groups who were opposed to the content of the curriculum.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: The decision to target middle school students (grades 6–8) was supported by research as the most appropriate level to provide the program. In addition, aspects found to be ineffective, including cognitive learning, fact retention, and testing, were avoided in favour of skill-based, active learning focussed on behavior change, and an incentive system.
participation_v1_1_v2: Some messaging may have appeared conflicting. For example, students were encouraged to not drink but were also provided advice on how to minimise harm if they did drink.
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: The program was described to be 'positively received'.

activity_script_v1_1: The HFL curriculum consisted of 54 lessons designed to be delivered either as one intensive 12-week program or as three separate four-week sessions for an entire cohort of middle school students. The program’s intensity was based on research suggesting that sustained intervention is necessary to create meaningful behaviour change. It incorporated eight key teaching strategies tailored to young adolescents, including practicing refusal skills in situations involving peer pressure, using peer leaders to promote health messages, involving parents through interviews about family values and rules, engaging students in community health-promotion activities, focusing on the immediate effects of unhealthy behaviours, analysing the influence of advertising and media, encouraging students to make public commitments to healthy behaviours while supporting one another, and providing accurate information about peer health behaviours to address misconceptions about social norms.
activity_delivery_details: Activity was implemented as intended - high fidelity
barriers_v1_1_v2: There may have been a lack of generalisability to other schools regarding societal beliefs, given the focus on one specific school. Some parents also reported resistance regarding the content of the proposed curriculum.
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: Program was "positively received"

activity_script_v1_1: The curriculum involved 15 weekly, 50-minute sessions during the spring school term. Based on a life skills training model, it used instruction, modelling and practice to develop cognitive-behavioural skills for preventing substance abuse, while being tailored to the cultural priorities and everyday experiences of Native American young people in western reservation communities. Group leaders and slightly older peers taught and demonstrated problem-solving, coping and interpersonal communication skills to help young people resist pressures to use substances in both Native and broader American society. Homework involved observing influences on substance use, such as alcohol and tobacco advertising, identifying ways people avoided substances, and considering strategies for promoting abstinence. Booster sessions (two, 50-minute sessions) were delivered semiannually.
activity_delivery_details: Intervention fidelity was assessed and described to correspond to written protocols.

activity_script_v1_1: The curriculum was designed through the use of theory and student feedback. The intensive program involved nine sessions delivered by trained school teachers and project staff. The sessions were delivered in sets of three sessions. The first set focussed on 'pro-health programming' and effective listening. The second set focussed on coping skills and education on drug related harms. The third set focussed on decision making and self management. In addition, a series of school meetings were held by student chairs that organised student services.

A total of 13 to 27 meetings were held across the schools and activity delivery was said to have been successful. activity: 2.1 Establishing a coalition and building its capacity
activity_script_v1_1: Partnerships were fostered between schools, police departments, treatment providers, local youth service organisations and other local organisations. Representatives from schools and police departments were asked to take the leadership role in project planning, governance, budgeting and implementation.
activity_delivery_details: A process evaluation reported different levels of participation in all the broader prevention activities. Many partners from mental health agencies withdrew from the partnerships due to resource priorities.
facilitators_v1_1_v2: Partnerships were reported to benefit when including 'nontraditional partners' such as the police department and city government representatives. With these member, some partnerships were able to achieve systemic change. However, it was important for partners to create a shared vision and to persevere despite "perils and difficulties". In addition, when members included police and government as well as a housing and community development corporation, partnerships were able to raise funds to continue the broader prevention program.

reference: Wolfson, M., Champion, H., Rogers, T., Neiberg, R. H., Barker, D. C., Talton, J. W., Ip, E. H., D’Agostino, R. B., Parries, M. T., & Easterling, D. (2011). Evaluation of free to grow: Head start partnerships to promote substance-free communities. Eval Rev, 35(2), 153–188.
activity_script_v1_1: Various activities centred around increasing social connectedness and introducing leadership opportunities throughout the participating communities. These activities were referred to as 'community action' and 'community-strengthening components'. In addition, several reports and communications were issued to the community as part of a broader awareness raising campaign.
activity_delivery_details: A process evaluation reported different levels of participation in all the broader prevention activities. Most partnerships conducted a 'knock and talk' campaign to speak with community members at their own home. Many partners from mental health agencies withdrew from the partnerships due to resource priorities.

reference: Wolfson, M., Champion, H., Rogers, T., Neiberg, R. H., Barker, D. C., Talton, J. W., Ip, E. H., D’Agostino, R. B., Parries, M. T., & Easterling, D. (2011). Evaluation of free to grow: Head start partnerships to promote substance-free communities. Eval Rev, 35(2), 153–188.
activity_script_v1_1: Representatives from schools and police departments were asked to take the leadership role in project planning, governance, budgeting and implementation. Partnerships were funded and supported by part-time project staff to conduct community needs assessments and choose and implement activities according to the identified risk and protective factors.
activity_delivery_details: A process evaluation reported different levels of participation in all the broader prevention activities. Many partners from mental health agencies withdrew from the partnerships due to resource priorities.
barriers_v1_1_v2: Initially project staff were hired as part-time consultants to provide technical assistance and reported difficulties. Over time the staff became full time and were described to provide "significantly more tailored and strategic" assistance.

reference: Wolfson, M., Champion, H., Rogers, T., Neiberg, R. H., Barker, D. C., Talton, J. W., Ip, E. H., D’Agostino, R. B., Parries, M. T., & Easterling, D. (2011). Evaluation of free to grow: Head start partnerships to promote substance-free communities. Eval Rev, 35(2), 153–188.
activity_script_v1_1: Participating schools implemented the 'Head Start' program. This program promotes school readiness by providing educational, health, nutritional, social and other services to preschool-age children and their families, mainly those with limited income. In addition, many participating schools allowed the community youth to use the schools as 'safe spaces'.
activity_delivery_details: A process evaluation reported different levels of participation in all the broader prevention activities.

reference: Wolfson, M., Champion, H., Rogers, T., Neiberg, R. H., Barker, D. C., Talton, J. W., Ip, E. H., D’Agostino, R. B., Parries, M. T., & Easterling, D. (2011). Evaluation of free to grow: Head start partnerships to promote substance-free communities. Eval Rev, 35(2), 153–188.
activity_script_v1_1: Participating communities implemented various activities designed to support families to keep their children free from alcohol and drug use ('family-strengthening strategies'). The activities included workshops, case management, and mentoring and were provided based on prior needs assessments.
activity_delivery_details: A process evaluation reported different levels of participation in all the broader prevention activities. By the end of the evaluation very few communities were rated to have a 'strong' focus on parenting.

reference: Schinke, S. P., Schwinn, T. M., Di Noia, J., & Cole, K. C. (2004). Reducing the risks of alcohol use among urban youth: Three-year effects of a computer-based intervention with and without parent involvement. J Stud Alcohol, 65(4), 443–449.
activity_script_v1_1:
Parenting activities included an initial 30-minute video with printed materials in English and Spanish. The video introduced the youth intervention, showed parents how to help their children apply its content to avoid alcohol-related problems, and highlighted family rituals, rules and bonding as prevention strategies. Parents also received two newsletters with child-management tips and movie and food coupons for watching the video.

In addition two-hour booster workshops were annually to review and expand on the video. Parents completed exercises with their children and returned a postcard about the exercise. Attendees also received a certificate and transport reimbursement. The workshops focused on reducing alcohol use and misuse and encouraged parent–child discussion of gender-specific pressures, such as girls being pressured by boyfriends to drink and boys drinking to demonstrate masculinity.
activity_delivery_details: The majority of parents (83%) watched the video, and attended the workshops (67%) and completed the exercises with their children (79%).

reference: Schinke, S. P., Schwinn, T. M., Di Noia, J., & Cole, K. C. (2004). Reducing the risks of alcohol use among urban youth: Three-year effects of a computer-based intervention with and without parent involvement. J Stud Alcohol, 65(4), 443–449.
activity_script_v1_1: This activity involved ten 45-minute CD-ROM sessions based on social learning and problem behaviour theories. The sessions covered goal setting, coping, peer pressure, refusal skills, norm correction, self-efficacy, problem solving, decision making, communication and time management. In a simulated urban setting, youths practised five problem-solving steps (Stop, Options, Decide, Act and Self-Praise) to identify alcohol-related problems, consider and select solutions, observe their consequences and reinforce successful problem solving. Animated characters reflected participants’ age, gender and ethnic-racial background. Subsequent 30-minute CD-ROM boosters reviewed earlier content.
activity_delivery_details: The majority (91%) of youths completed the CD-ROM sessions.

reference: Schinke, S. P., Schwinn, T. M., Di Noia, J., & Cole, K. C. (2004). Reducing the risks of alcohol use among urban youth: Three-year effects of a computer-based intervention with and without parent involvement. J Stud Alcohol, 65(4), 443–449.
activity_script_v1_1: At first, parents were shown a 30-minute video (in Spanish and in English) and presented with physical materials informing them of the intervention and the ways in which they can help prevent alcohol use among their children by instilling strong social and family norms and values. Parents were also provided with child management information and advice via newsletters. The information provided in the videotape and physical materials were expanded upon via a 2-hour workshop (also in Spanish and in English), and they were provided with a manual they could take home to encourage further delivery and maintenance of the skills learnt. Parents also received booster sessions where they directly engaged with the CD-ROM programs.
activity_delivery_details: Most parents watched the videotape (n=163, 83%), attended the workshop (n=131, 67%) and completed the CD-ROM activity with their children (n=155, 79%)

reference: Schinke, S. P., Schwinn, T. M., Di Noia, J., & Cole, K. C. (2004). Reducing the risks of alcohol use among urban youth: Three-year effects of a computer-based intervention with and without parent involvement. J Stud Alcohol, 65(4), 443–449.
activity_script_v1_1: CD-ROM program (45-minutes long) underpinned by social learning and problem behaviour theories, with a focus on social norms, peer pressure coping, communication, managing time, collectively designed to prevent alcohol use among youths. Each session was shaped around particular goals and objectives, and these activities were communicated via animations that were demographically similar to the youths engaging in the activities. Stop, Options, Decide, Act and Self-Praise problem-solving steps were applied by youths in each session.
activity_delivery_details: Most youths completed the CD-ROM sessions (91%)

activity_script_v1_1:
Students in local public schools in the fourth grade received the "I’m Special" program which comprised eight one-hour sessions delivered three times a year. It focused on personal values, self-esteem, decision-making, problem-solving, coping and group cooperation skills. 

Students in grades five to nine received the "Ombudsman" program which was delivered in approximately 50-minute sessions twice a week each semester. The program involved three phases: developing self-awareness and personal values; building communication, decision-making and problem-solving skills; and applying these skills through a school or community project as student ‘Ombudsmen’.
activity_delivery_details: Over two years, approximately 1,583 students participated in the fourth grade and 480 students participated in grades five to nine.

reference: Kim, S. (1982). Feeder area approach: An impact evaluation of a prevention project on student drug abuse. International Journal of the Addictions, 17(2), 305–313.
activity_script_v1_1: Teachers and school administrators were offered 10 training modules designed to strengthen their capacity to support young people’s social development. These included Teacher Effectiveness Training (30 hours), Affective Educational Goal Setting (30 hours), and Ombudsman Training (20 hours; covering self-awareness, communication and school or community project development). Other modules addressed practical approaches to drug education, teacher wellbeing, school discipline, motivation, classroom management and student self-esteem (three to 10 hours each), as well as Creative Use of Opposition (20 hours), which focused on responses to conflict, anger management and creative conflict resolution.
activity_delivery_details: Administrative difficulties were encountered during the project and the activities were not implemented "as much as expected at the beginning of the project".

reference: Kim, S. (1982). Feeder area approach: An impact evaluation of a prevention project on student drug abuse. International Journal of the Addictions, 17(2), 305–313.
activity_script_v1_1: Parents were offered 11 programs, supported by two full-time staff members and five interns working in low-income neighbourhood centres. Programs included Parent Effectiveness Training (24 hours), which developed communication, problem-solving, conflict management and parenting skills; Discipline at Home (eight hours), focused on preventing and managing children’s problem behaviours; and Parenting of Youth (four to five hours), which addressed issues arising during early adolescence. Other programs covered stress management (six hours), separation and divorce (eight hours), stepparenting (six hours), assertiveness (eight hours), financial management (two hours), drug information (two hours), and talking with children about drugs (two hours).
activity_delivery_details: Administrative difficulties were encountered during the project and the activities were not implemented "as much as expected at the beginning of the project".

reference: Rotheram-Borus, M. J., Tomlinson, M., Durkin, A., Baird, K., DeCelles, J., & Swendeman, D. (2016). Feasibility of Using Soccer and Job Training to Prevent Drug Abuse and HIV. AIDS Behav, 20(9), 1841–1850.
activity_script_v1_1: Grassroot Soccer (GRS) was a soccer-based prevention intervention for young men in township neighbourhoods in sub-Saharan Africa. Coaches from different neighbourhoods were trained in evidence-based behaviour-change skills, including goal setting, problem-solving, role-playing, coping, emotional self-control and assertive social behaviours, as well as referral to local health and community services. During twice-weekly soccer practices and Saturday games, coaches used discussion and role-play to address alcohol and drug use, HIV and other health issues, healthy routines, supportive social networks, respectful relationships with women and violence. Coaches also monitored attendance, punctuality, sportsmanship and participation in random alcohol and drug screening, and referred participants experiencing substance use problems to health clinics.
activity_delivery_details: Participants attended most (71%) of the soccer trainings and games (the mean number of practices/games attended was 47.3 [SD = 34.4]).
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: Participants found the soccer activities engaging (more engaging than the community education).

reference: Rotheram-Borus, M. J., Tomlinson, M., Durkin, A., Baird, K., DeCelles, J., & Swendeman, D. (2016). Feasibility of Using Soccer and Job Training to Prevent Drug Abuse and HIV. AIDS Behav, 20(9), 1841–1850.
activity_script_v1_1: Participants who showed attendance to the broader prevention program were offered an eight-week electrical or mechanical engineering course at a local college, held twice weekly. Participants received necessary equipment and materials and gained practical experience enabling participants to apply for entry-level employment or establish a small informal business. The intention of this education was to promote a social and personal identity that values responsible, respectful relationships.
activity_delivery_details: Just under half of the participants (48%) attended a workshop with a low graduation rate (34%).
satistfaction_v1_1_v2: Participants did not find the community education to be engaging.
